catalog_quote: [p.13] Like English, Yugambeh is 'stress-timed', as are the other dialects of this language. The prominent syllables and words take more time, and the unstressed words and syllables are often slurred over. ... [p.14] You should note that the first syllable of a word is usually stressed and clear, except when there is a long vowel elsewhere in the word, which then gets the primary stress, and the first syllable is less clear. ... [p.16] You will note that there are long and short vowels. Short e is rather rare, although it sometimes alternates with i or a word finally. Unstressed vowels in the language lose their 'colour', as they do in English. Long vowels (all the ones with h written after them) are stressed; otherwise the first syllable of a word is stressed. There are never (or almost never) two long vowels in a row.

new_statements.quote: A syllable contains as nucleus a vowel with or without length. Stress occurs on the first syllable of the word, or on the first long syllable if such is present. Syllable patterns are of the form CV(:)(C), and words contain from one to five syllables. [p. 75] ... Contiguous long syllables are avoided in the language in almost all cases. When consecutive syllables with long nuclei would occur, the even syllables, numbering from the first long syllable, are shortened. [p. 77] ... Culham pronounced the negative yugambe: or yugumbe: (the second syllable has little stress and the vowel is a little obscure) [p. 96]

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog lists Yugambeh with an empty rule and no existing statements; this source supplies the placement: initial by default, but attracted to the first long vowel (weight-sensitive, quantity = vowel length). NB the Rosetta Project split the work into sections; the listed open_url (rosettaproject_bdy_references-1) is the bibliography section and the stress statement is in rosettaproject_bdy_phon-1. M. C. Cunningham is the same person as Margaret C. Sharpe (author of works 1 and 2).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress goes on the first long (V:) syllable of the word if there is one; otherwise on the initial syllable. Vowel length is phonemic (/:/), and a morphophonemic rule shortens every second long syllable counting from the first long one, so adjacent long syllables almost never occur; this keeps the 'first long syllable' rule unambiguous. Words have one to five syllables, roots at most four.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed. The only related remark is that the second syllable of the negative yugambe:/yugumbe: 'has little stress and the vowel is a little obscure' (p. 96), which is an observation about a single word, not a rule.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for stress itself. For the long-syllable avoidance rule that feeds it, bu:ye:n 'tired' 'appears to be an exception' (p. 77, past-tense allomorph discussion), and a hypothetical /e:/ created by affixation surfaces short where it would give contiguous long syllables (p. 75).
new_statements.identity_note: Cunningham 1969 describes the Yugumbir (Yugambeh) dialect of Bandjalang as spoken by Joe Culham (with data from Mrs Weizel and from Geytenbeek and Watson), i.e. the northern (Logan-Albert) end of the Tweed-Albert chain, Glottolog dialect yugu1249 under twee1234. M. C. Cunningham is the maiden-name byline of Margaret C. Sharpe, so all three listed works are by the same author. Sharpe 2020 covers the Mibiny varieties Yugambeh, Ngarahngwal and Ngahnduwal (Tweed to Logan), which are the dialects of twee1234; Sharpe 2005 covers the whole Yugambeh-Bundjalung chain including varieties outside twee1234.

tone.quote: [p.413, 9.6] Stress is - as in all Australian languages studied by the present author - not distinctive. A tendency persists, however, especially in words or contexts of at least three syllables to slightly emphasise, or stress, the second initial syllable, as for instance in the word warmerigan white woman, which is often heard as war me'rigan (Man GC, ML; cf. Part I, 2.9) ... otherwise we adopt the principle (mentioned in 9.2) of not marking non-initial vowels as long. [p.5, Part I 2.9] Stress is not significant in any of the languages dealt with in this survey. Still a certain tendency persists everywhere to stress the vowel of the second initial syllable in words or utterances of some length

tone.summary: No tone mentioned; stress described as non-distinctive with a second-syllable tendency; vowel length contrastive (marked only in initial syllables).

tone.quote: Accent :—Words of two syllables when ending in a vowel are accented on the first syllable ; when ending in a consonant the two syllables are equally sounded. Words of three syllables generally have the accent on the first syllable, with a secondary accent on the last syllable if the word ends in a consonant. In words with vowel endings the accent is often on the penultimate. The acute accent is used to mark exceptions from these rules.

tone.quote: [p.364] From anecdotal evidence from descendants of speakers, and from one older speaker of Gidhabal (Boyd pers. comm.) there were almost certainly changes in voice quality, overall pitch and intonation, and perhaps in rate of utterance from place to place. [p.372] Watson in particular uses some diacritics on certain vowels. An acute accent indicates stress usually when it falls on other than the first syllable. By Crowley's, the Geytenbeeks' and my analysis, this indicates a long vowel in the syllable perceived as stressed.

tone.quote: [p.45, 6.3 STRESS] Stress (extra loudness) occurs on the first syllable of a word, or if a later syllable is long (has a long vowel), then it will be heard on the long vowel. It is sometimes easier to hear the stress than the length, so if a second or third syllable sounds louder, it almost certainly has a long vowel. If a two-syllable word has a long vowel in the second syllable, sometimes the first syllable gets stressed anyway. [p.51, 7.3] Any statement in this language can be turned into a question by changing the intonation. A statement is said in Yugambeh-Bundjalung with the voice pitch falling at the end ... A question in Yugambeh-Bundjalung is asked by the voice pitch rising at the end, unless there is a question word like nyang ‘what’
tone.locator: Section 6.3 'Stress', p.45; section 7.3 'Yes/no questions', p.51; index: 'Stress or loudness 45', 'intonation 51, 112-114'
tone.summary: No tone described: word prosody is stress (first syllable, or on a long vowel later in the word) plus contrastive vowel length; pitch functions only as sentence intonation (falling statements, rising yes/no questions and tags).
